worksheet.title: First, Next, Last
worksheet.subtitle: Putting steps in the right order
worksheet.learning_goal: I can put steps in order: first, next, last.

parts.title: Steps happen in order
parts.text: When we do something, the steps happen in order: first, next, last. Bit is building a block tower — one block, then two, then three.

parts.title: Watch Bit build — in order
parts.note: First 1 block, next 2 blocks, last 3 blocks. The tower grows in order.

parts.title: Which step is FIRST?
parts.prompt: The first step has the fewest dots. Circle the step that comes FIRST.

parts.title: Which step is LAST?
parts.prompt: The last step has the most dots. Circle the step that comes LAST.

parts.title: You try — write the order
parts.prompt: Write 1, 2, 3 under the mixed-up steps to put them in order (fewest to most).

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Doing steps in the right order — first, next, last — is how we follow a plan. A plan made of ordered steps is called an algorithm.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Children put the steps of an action in order — first, next, last — using cards with fewer or more dots. Putting steps in the right order is the start of a plan (an algorithm). No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil or crayon. You read each prompt aloud; the child answers by circling or numbering. Optional: real objects or cards to put in order by hand first.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 15 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Line up cards with 1, 2, 3 dots: "fewest comes first, most comes last."
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — the card with one dot comes first.
3. Let them try. Children do Exercise 2 (last), then Exercise 3 (number them 1, 2, 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — circle the single-dot card (fewest = first). Exercise 2 — circle the three-dot card (most = last).
Exercise 3 — order is: one dot = 1, two dots = 2, three dots = 3.

parts.title: If children get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: ordering by where a card sits on the page, not by the number of dots. Count the dots together.
Make it easier: line up real objects from fewest to most by hand first.
Make it harder: add a fourth card (four dots) and order all four.
Make it active: have three children hold 1, 2, 3 dots and line themselves up.

parts.title: Ontario Kindergarten link (official wording)
text: Problem Solving and Innovating — children order the steps of a familiar process.
In plain terms: putting the steps of an action in order — first, next, last.
No reading is needed from the child — you read each prompt aloud; the child answers by circling, numbering, or drawing arrows.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child orders the cards from fewest to most and labels them 1, 2, 3.
